lesson.title: Give Your Errors a Name: Writing Custom Exceptions
lesson.summary: A custom exception is a small class, built by subclassing Exception, that gives a specific problem in your program its own descriptive name instead of forcing it to reuse a generic built in type.
lesson.body:
ValueError works fine for a single rule like a negative age, but it starts to feel vague once a program has several unrelated validation rules, each one raising ValueError with a different message, and every except ValueError block ends up catching all of them indiscriminately whether it means to or not. Custom exceptions solve this by letting a program define its own exception types, each one naming a specific problem clearly. Since exceptions are just classes, defining one uses exactly the class syntax already covered, applied to a very small class that inherits from Python's built in Exception.

```python
class InsufficientFundsError(Exception):
    """Raised when a withdrawal exceeds the account balance."""
    pass

def withdraw(balance, amount):
    if amount > balance:
        raise InsufficientFundsError(
            f"Cannot withdraw {amount}: balance is only {balance}"
        )
    return balance - amount

print(withdraw(100, 40))

try:
    withdraw(100, 150)
except InsufficientFundsError as error:
    print(f"Transaction blocked: {error}")
```

withdraw(100, 40) checks 40 > 100, which is False, so it returns 100 - 40, which is 60, printed directly. The try block then calls withdraw(100, 150), which checks 150 > 100, True, and raises InsufficientFundsError with the message "Cannot withdraw 150: balance is only 100". The except clause matches that exact custom type, catches it, binds it to error, and str(error) inside the f-string produces the message text that was passed in when the exception was created. Output:

```
60
Transaction blocked: Cannot withdraw 150: balance is only 100
```

class InsufficientFundsError(Exception): says this new class inherits everything a normal exception needs, message handling, traceback behavior, the ability to be raised and caught, from Exception, its parent class. The body can be as small as pass, since most custom exceptions do not need any new methods or attributes of their own, they exist purely to give a category of error a distinct, readable name. That name is what makes tracebacks self documenting: InsufficientFundsError tells the next reader exactly what kind of problem occurred, without needing to open the code or parse a generic message string.

Custom exceptions also make except blocks more precise. except InsufficientFundsError only catches that specific problem, leaving unrelated errors, like a TypeError from a bad argument, to propagate normally, which is exactly the kind of narrow, deliberate matching that multiple except blocks are built for. Larger programs commonly define several related custom exceptions, sometimes even inheriting from a shared custom base exception, so that code calling into a module can choose to catch either one very specific failure, or the whole family of failures that module might raise.
